title: Gemstones
directAnswer: A gem element is a kind of mineral that appears in every rock. Take the set of distinct letters in the first rock, then intersect it with the letter-set of each remaining rock. Whatever survives all the intersections is present in every rock — its size is the answer. Equivalently, count how many of the 26 letters appear in all rocks. O(total characters) time, O(1) space (26-letter alphabet).

remember.pattern: Set intersection across all rows / per-letter universal count
rules: A gem must appear in **every** rock — one rock missing a letter eliminates it for good.
Use **distinct** letters per rock; repeats inside a single rock don't matter.
Intersection only shrinks the set — start with rock 0 and keep `&=`-ing the rest.
Equivalent counting form: a letter is a gem iff its **per-letter count of rocks containing it** equals the number of rocks.
The alphabet is fixed (a–z), so a `boolean[26]` per rock or a `int[26]` tally gives O(1) space.
whenToUse: You need elements common to *all* of several collections (intersection of many sets)
The universe is a small fixed alphabet so sets become boolean[26] tables
Duplicates within one collection are irrelevant — only presence matters
'Appears in every…' phrasing is a tell for whole-set intersection
antiSignals: You need elements in *any* rock (union) → union, not intersection
Counts across rocks matter (e.g. 'appears at least k times total') → frequency, not presence
Order or position matters → this is no longer a pure set problem
The alphabet is huge/unknown → real hash sets instead of boolean[26]
remember.takeaway: 'Common to all' is set intersection; fold it across the collection with `&=`, starting from the first element's set. With a fixed 26-letter alphabet, a per-letter 'in how many rocks?' tally is the same idea in O(1) space — a gem is any letter whose tally equals the rock count.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you map 'appears in every rock' onto a set intersection (or a per-letter universal-count), and whether you correctly use distinct letters per rock so within-rock repeats don't skew the result.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Counting total occurrences of each letter across all rocks and comparing to the number of rocks — a letter appearing twice in one rock and zero times in another would wrongly hit the threshold.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Offer the O(1)-space counting version: one int[26] where slot c counts how many rocks contain letter c (deduped per rock); the answer is the number of slots equal to the rock count.

problemStatement:
You are given an array of `n` rocks, each represented by a non-empty string of lowercase letters. Each letter inside a rock is a **mineral**.

A mineral is called a **gem element** (or gemstone) if it occurs **at least once in every rock**.

Return the number of distinct gem elements — that is, how many letters appear in all `n` rocks.
constraints: Each rock string consists of lowercase English letters a–z
understanding: Think of each rock as the *set* of letters it contains (repeats collapse away). A gemstone is a letter that belongs to all of those sets at once — the intersection of every rock's letter-set. The count of that intersection is the answer. Because there are only 26 possible letters, you can track this with a fixed-size table instead of general sets.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does a repeated letter inside one rock count more than once?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Only presence matters per rock, so deduplicate each rock to its distinct letters first.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must a gem appear in EVERY rock, or just most?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Every rock. A single rock lacking the letter disqualifies it entirely.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could a rock be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Per the constraints each rock is non-empty; if an empty rock were allowed, the intersection would be empty and the answer 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the alphabet limited to a–z?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, lowercase English letters. That fixed 26-letter universe lets us use a boolean[26]/int[26] instead of hash sets.

examples.explanation: Letters in all three: 'a' (yes/yes/yes) and 'b' (yes/yes/yes). 'c' is missing from the third rock, 'd'/'e'/'g' fail somewhere. Two gemstones.
Only 's' appears in all four rocks. Everything else is missing from at least one.
With a single rock, every distinct letter in it is a gemstone: a, b, c.

approaches.name: Test Each Letter Against Every Rock (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: State it first — it reads straight off the definition, then note it rescans rocks for all 26 letters.
hints: The definition says a gem is in every rock. How would you verify that for one candidate letter?
For each letter from 'a' to 'z', check whether it appears in every rock by scanning each rock.
Count the letters that pass the 'present in all rocks' test. That count is the answer.
approaches.complexityReasoning: For each of the 26 letters you may scan every rock fully, so the work is 26 × (sum of rock lengths) in the worst case. Only a counter is stored → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Translate the definition directly: a gemstone is a letter present in all rocks, so test the 26 candidate letters one at a time. For a letter `c`, walk each rock and ask 'does this rock contain `c`?'. If every rock answers yes, `c` is a gem; tally it.

**Why it is correct.** It is the definition expressed as nested loops — letters on the outside, rocks on the inside. There's no insight to overlook, which makes it a clean way to confirm you understand 'present in every rock'.

**Why deduping within a rock is irrelevant here.** Because the inner test is membership ('does the rock contain `c`?'), repeats inside a rock don't matter — `contains` is the same whether `c` appears once or five times. That's the same reason the optimal version works on distinct letters.

**Why we don't ship it.** For each of the 26 letters you potentially rescan every rock from scratch, repeating the same character reads up to 26 times. You can instead make one pass per rock, record its *distinct* letters, and combine those across rocks. Mention this as the literal reading, give the `O(26 · total)` cost, then move to the intersection / counting solution.
approaches.insight: Each candidate-letter scan re-reads characters it has already seen. Recording each rock's distinct letters once and intersecting (or tallying) them removes that repetition — you read every character a single time.

Assuming indexOf / `in` is O(1) — each call scans the rock.
Confusing 'present in every rock' (intersection) with 'present in some rock' (union).

approaches.name: Set Intersection / Per-Letter Universal Count (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer. Say 'intersect each rock's distinct letters' or 'count letters present in all n rocks'.
hints: Flip the loops: instead of asking each letter about every rock, process each rock once and remember its distinct letters. What operation combines those per-rock letter sets into 'present in all'?
Seed a 'common' set with the distinct letters of the first rock, then intersect it with each later rock's letter set. Intersection only removes letters, never adds.
Or count, per letter, how many rocks contain it (dedupe within a rock first). A letter is a gem exactly when that count equals the number of rocks. Answer = number of such letters.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each character of each rock is read once to build per-rock presence → O(total characters). The state is a fixed 26-slot table (or a set of ≤26 letters), independent of input size → O(1) auxiliary space.
approaches.explanation:
Process the rocks once. Maintain the set of letters common to all rocks seen so far, starting from the first rock's distinct letters, and intersect it with each subsequent rock. The size of what remains is the gemstone count.

**Why intersection is the right operation.** 'Appears in every rock' is, by definition, membership in the intersection of all the per-rock letter sets. Folding intersection across the rocks (`common = common ∩ rock_letters`) keeps exactly the letters that have appeared in every rock processed so far. Intersection is monotone-shrinking: a letter, once dropped because some rock lacked it, can never come back — which matches the rule that one missing rock disqualifies a gem permanently.

**Why distinct letters per rock.** The intersection cares only about presence, so collapse each rock to its set of distinct letters first. A letter appearing five times in one rock contributes the same as appearing once; deduping avoids letting within-rock repeats distort anything.

**The equivalent counting view (and why it's O(1) space).** Keep an `int[26]` where slot `c` counts *how many rocks contain `c`*. For each rock, take its distinct letters and bump those slots by one. After all rocks, a letter is a gem exactly when its slot equals `n`, the number of rocks — it showed up in every one. Counting the slots equal to `n` gives the answer. The table is fixed at 26 entries regardless of how many or how long the rocks are, so the extra space is constant. **Deduping per rock is what makes the threshold check valid** — without it, two occurrences in a single rock would push the count toward `n` dishonestly.

**Why both views are the same algorithm.** The intersection set is precisely the set of letters whose per-rock count reached `n`. One expresses it as repeated set ANDs, the other as a tally with a final threshold — pick whichever reads more clearly in the interview.
approaches.insight: 'Common to all collections' is the textbook signal for set intersection folded across the inputs. When the element universe is a small fixed alphabet, swap the hash set for a per-letter 'in how many rocks?' counter: it's the same intersection in O(1) space, and the gem test becomes 'count == number of rocks'.

pitfalls: Counting total occurrences across rocks instead of deduping per rock — a doubled letter in one rock can fake the threshold.
Starting the intersection from an empty set instead of rock 0's letters — yields 0 every time.
Using union (any rock) instead of intersection (every rock).

commonMistakes: Counting how many times each letter appears in total and comparing to the rock count, without deduping within each rock.
Computing the union of letters (present in some rock) instead of the intersection (present in all).
Seeding the 'common' set as empty rather than from the first rock.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Total occurrences instead of per-rock presence
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you count every occurrence, a letter appearing twice in rock A and never in rock B can reach the rock-count threshold and be wrongly called a gem. Dedupe each rock first.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Union instead of intersection
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Using |= (union) collects letters present in ANY rock, which counts far too many. Gems must be in EVERY rock, which is intersection (&=).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Seeding the intersection empty
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Intersecting an empty set with anything stays empty, so you'd always return 0. Seed with the first rock's distinct letters, then intersect the rest.

patternNote: Set intersection across many collections. 'Present in every collection' folds intersection across the inputs, seeded by the first one. When the universe is a small fixed alphabet, replace the hash set with a per-letter 'in how many collections?' counter — a gem is any letter whose count equals the number of collections — giving O(1) space. Same shape as Find Common Characters and multi-array intersection.
